task_row_model.query: Classify convergence (absolute, conditional, or divergence) of the series sum_{n=1}^∞ (-1)^n n^\u03b1/(n+1) depending on the real parameter α. Specify the ranges of α for each behavior and give the minimal justification.

documents.content: In real-analysis courses the p-series test is a basic criterion: the series sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-p} converges precisely when p>1 and diverges for p\le 1. This is typically proved by comparison with the integral of x^{-p} or by the Cauchy condensation test. The criterion is stable under limit comparison: if a_n\sim C n^{-p} with C>0 then sum a_n has the same convergence behavior as the p-series. Many standard texts present this as the benchmark for comparing polynomial-power tails of sequences.
documents.reasoning_trace: Provides the p-series convergence threshold (converges iff p>1) and justifies using limit or comparison tests for sequences asymptotic to n^{-p}.

documents.content: Consider the sequence b_n(\u03b1)=n^{\u03b1}/(n+1). For fixed real \u03b1 one has b_n(\u03b1)=n^{\u03b1-1}\cdot(1+1/n)^{-1}, so b_n(\u03b1)\sim n^{\u03b1-1} as n\to\infty; equivalently the ratio b_n/n^{\u03b1-1} tends to 1. Hence b_n(\u03b1)\to 0 exactly when \u03b1-1<0, i.e. \u03b1<1. For these \u03b1 the function f(x)=x^{\u03b1}/(x+1) is eventually decreasing in x, so the discrete sequence is eventually monotone decreasing for large n when \u03b1<1.
documents.reasoning_trace: Gives asymptotic equivalence b_n ~ n^{\u03b1-1}, the necessary condition for termwise limit to be zero (\u03b1<1), and asserts eventual monotonicity needed for alternating-series application.

documents.content: The alternating series test states: if (c_n) is a sequence of positive terms that is monotonically decreasing to 0, then the alternating series sum (-1)^n c_n converges. Absolute convergence means sum |a_n| converges; otherwise, if sum a_n converges but sum |a_n| diverges, the convergence is conditional. The test does not require checking absolute convergence; it only requires eventual monotone decrease and vanishing of the terms.
documents.reasoning_trace: Supplies the alternating series test criteria (decreasing to zero implies convergence) and defines conditional versus absolute convergence.

documents.content: Alternating sums have a long anecdotal history: Leibniz used the alternating harmonic series in the 17th century to estimate pi/4, and later Euler explored many divergent-series summation methods. Journalistic overviews often highlight historical personalities and speculative links to physics, but these narratives frequently mix rigorous statements with intuitive commentary. While interesting, the biographies and speculative connections do not alter the elementary convergence tests used in analysis courses.

Applied mathematics reports sometimes discuss the practical rate of convergence of alternating series and error bounds from first omitted term, especially in computational contexts. They may present examples where truncation after N terms gives an error bounded by the next term's magnitude when terms are monotone decreasing. Such computational notes restate standard theorems about error control and are primarily concerned with numerical estimates rather than classification thresholds.

task_row_model.golden_answer: Let a_n = (-1)^n n^{\u03b1}/(n+1). Since n^{\u03b1}/(n+1) ~ n^{\u03b1-1}, |a_n| behaves like n^{\u03b1-1}; by the p-series test |a_n| sums iff \u03b1-1<-1, i.e. \u03b1<0, so absolute convergence occurs for \u03b1<0. For \u03b1<1 the terms tend to 0 and are eventually decreasing, so the alternating series converges; combining with above yields conditional convergence for 0\u2264\u03b1<1. For \u03b1\u22651 the terms do not tend to zero, so the series diverges.
